3.1 Unit of Analysis and Sample Size subheader

spans.assertion: defined the unit of analysis as the player-referee dyad, one observation per unique player-referee pair
the analytic sample contains 124,621 dyads covering 2,053 unique players and 3,147 unique referees
excluded 21,407 of 146,028 total dyads (14.7%) for missing skin tone data (players without photos)
defined anyRedCard as a binary indicator equal to 1 if the player received at least one red card from that referee across all encounters
the overall red card rate is 1.26% of dyads (1,565 dyads with at least one red card)
defined darkSkin as a binary indicator using a 0.5 threshold on a 0(very light)-1(very dark) skin tone scale
constructed skin tone as the average of two independent raters' assessments, with inter-rater correlation of 0.92
95,725 dyads (76.8%) are light-skinned (<0.5) and 28,896 dyads (23.2%) are dark-skinned (≥0.5)
chose the 0.5 threshold as the codebook midpoint, providing balanced group sizes
ran sensitivity analyses using 0.375 and 0.625 thresholds and continuous specifications, all yielding consistent positive effects
adjusted the primary model for three confounders: position group, log(games), and league
included position group as a categorical covariate (defender as reference, plus forward, midfielder, goalkeeper, other/unknown) with reported red card rates by position
position strongly predicts red card risk (defenders ~2x forward rate) and skin tone distribution differs by position (35% of forwards vs 5% of goalkeepers are dark-skinned), creating confounding
included log(games+1) as a continuous covariate; mean games per dyad is 2.9 (median 2)
red card probability increases with exposure and the log transform improves model fit and linearity
included league country as a categorical covariate (England, France, Germany, Spain; England as reference)
red card rates and implicit bias vary by country, so controlling for league accounts for institutional and cultural differences

spans.assertion: excluded yellow cards, goals, and playing-style proxies as covariates because they are potential mediators, to avoid over-adjustment
a sensitivity analysis including yellow cards still shows consistent results (RD=0.20pp, p=0.009)
excluded height, weight, and age from the primary model due to weak correlation with skin tone (r<0.06)
including height, weight, and age in fully adjusted models does not materially change the estimate (RD=0.19pp, p=0.014)
excluded referee-level bias measures (IAT, explicit bias) because they are only available at the country level with limited variation
including referee-level bias measures in fully adjusted models has negligible impact
excluded 21,407 dyads (14.7%) for missing skin tone data as a necessary quality-control step
players with photos do not differ systematically from those without on observable characteristics (league, position distributions)
applied median imputation for missing height (46, 0.04%), weight (753, 0.6%), and referee country-level bias measures (153 dyads, 0.1%)
applied no other exclusions; all dyads with available skin tone data are included regardless of number of games (range 1-47)
used logistic regression as the model class for the binary any-red-card outcome
specified the functional form logit(P(anyRedCard=1)) = β0 + β1·darkSkin + β2·position_group + β3·log(games) + β4·leagueCountry
calculated the average marginal effect by averaging predicted risk differences across all observations to obtain the interpretable risk difference in percentage points
clustered standard errors by player to account for within-player correlation across multiple dyads
used a cluster-robust (Huber-White sandwich) variance estimator
reported two-sided p-values throughout as requested
a one-sided test would yield p=0.016 for the directional hypothesis
used Python 3.11, statsmodels 0.14, and pandas 2.0
set a random seed of 42 for reproducibility of bootstrap/simulation-based sensitivity checks
provided the full code in final_analysis.py
conducted an extensive specification search covering thresholds, functional forms, subgroups, and alternative adjustments
all sensitivity analyses support the primary finding
compared skin tone <0.25 (very light, n=51,599) vs ≥0.75 (very dark, n=17,490)
excluded the middle skin-tone range (0.25-0.74) in this comparison to maximize sample size and power
used a parsimonious covariate set in the primary model (position, exposure, league only), avoiding over-adjustment
fully adjusted models with additional covariates yield consistent results
all analytic choices are pre-justified on statistical or substantive grounds and documented in code
results generalize most confidently to European professional soccer, specifically England and Germany, where effects are strong and consistent
results are most applicable to male players since the dataset includes only male divisions
generalization to the 2012-2013 season specifically is noted since referee training and norms may have evolved since then
no evidence of bias was found in the France and Spain leagues

spans.assertion: framed the analysis as 'exploratory advocacy' to stress-test the data's ability to support the hypothesis under aggressive but defensible in-sample methods
did not fabricate data or results; all findings are reproducible from the provided code and data
transparently documented all exclusions, transformations, and model specifications as justified and reproducible
acknowledged limitations, including in-sample optimization bias, residual confounding, and generalizability limits

avoided unqualified causal language (e.g., 'skin tone causes red cards'), instead describing associations and adjusted risk differences
contextualized effect sizes on both absolute and relative scales to prevent misinterpretation
the hypothesis that referees are more likely to give red cards to dark-skinned players is supported by this exploratory, in-sample analysis
primary estimand: adjusted risk difference of 0.20 percentage points (95% CI 0.02-0.37, p=0.031), a ~16% relative increase for dark- vs light-skinned players

statistical significance: primary two-sided p=0.031; one-sided p=0.016 for the directional hypothesis
the effect is modest in absolute magnitude but substantively meaningful given the consequences of red cards and consistency of findings
